A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ORSO and contain readable main text, algorithms, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–H. Retained, revised, and added material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments on six Isaac Gym tasks, including selection-algorithm comparisons, budget and candidate-set studies, and training traces.

after.justification: v3 retains these experiments and adds estimated GPU timing comparisons and original evaluations of all 96 reward candidates in the ANT selection study.

M1.justification: The reward-generation, separate-policy training, online selection, rejection-sampling, and iterative-refinement procedures remain unchanged. Appendix F retains the half-evolved, half-new resampling scheme. Omitting N from some pseudocode calls does not establish a procedural change, since the implementation retains the same update interval.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Cartpole, BallBalance, Ant, Humanoid, AllegroHand, and ShadowHand with the same task definitions. The large-candidate-set ANT scenario already exists in v1. Additional GPU configurations and candidate-wise evaluations do not introduce new task or environment coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain No Design, Human, Naive/EUREKA, EG, ETC, UCB, Exp3, and uniform selection where previously used. Although v3 shortens the main-text baseline description, Appendix H.2 explicitly identifies the naive strategy as EUREKA. The candidate-ranking analysis adds no new selection algorithm.

E3.justification: v3 replaces normalized cumulative regret with per-round normalized regret and replaces threshold-crossing summaries with reward-versus-budget curves. It also introduces timing estimates across 1–16 GPUs and independent evaluation of all 96 ANT candidates. PPO, the principal interaction budgets, and candidate-set sizes remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix H.1 adds a direct check of selection quality by evaluating every ANT reward candidate and marking those selected by D3RB. Figures 3 and 11 add resource-scaling analysis against parallel naive selection. These extend validation of the central selection and efficiency claims; existing ablations and training case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Most aggregate plots switch from 95% confidence intervals to standard errors, while the new Table 3 reports five-seed 95% confidence intervals. Existing three-seed main configurations and five-seed large-set experiments remain. v3's 27 runs per task correspond to v1's 162 runs across six tasks, rather than an increase.

E6.justification: v3 adds GPU timing results and candidate-wise ANT scores, including reward 34 at 10.24 ± 0.36 in Table 3. It replaces learning and regret summaries under revised metrics and explicitly reports a 56% advantage over naive selection at B = 15. These additions do not establish a same-setting performance improvement between versions.

T1.justification: Appendix B corrects the cumulative learner-reward sum to use each round's policy value rather than the final round's value. Appendix D makes the induction base case and hypotheses explicit. Assumption 4.2, Lemma 4.4's bound, and the substantive regret-balancing argument remain unchanged.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds reaching human performance at least twice as fast. v3 instead headlines more than 50% higher performance and up to eightfold computational savings, supported in the results by the 56% highest-budget comparison and GPU timing estimates. This substantially revises the empirical contribution claims while retaining the method and regret-guarantee claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds explicit tested candidate-set limits, recommends eight candidates with larger interaction budgets, and identifies parallel ORSO as future work. It qualifies the timing results as approximations and interprets Table 3 as validation of reward selection. The limitation concerning reliance on predefined task rewards is retained.

D1.justification: New Appendix E.1 supplies selected reward-function code for all six tasks, substantially expanding inspectable technical detail beyond v1's task and human-reward definitions. v3 also updates the repository pointer and removes the animated-visualization link. The existing selection hyperparameters and implementation procedures remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: The new main-text related-work section adds a distinction from restless bandits, citing Whittle, Weber and Weiss, and Gittins and colleagues. Additional citations cover sparse rewards and inverse reward design. Much of the section summarizes material already present in the retained Appendix A, so the positioning expansion is limited.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, reward-selection motivation, and results narrative are substantially rewritten. v3 reorganizes the explanation around exploration tradeoffs, interaction budgets, and GPU resources, adds main-text related work, and expands the limitations and appendix organization. Much of the algorithmic and proof text remains intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from two regret illustrations to three selection-strategy panels. Main and appendix summary plots are redrawn with revised axes, legends, colors, and panel arrangements. GPU charts, the candidate-ranking table, and boxed code listings are added. The existing training-trace figures are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: The selected reward listings and exhaustive ANT candidate check improve transparency and support selection quality beyond v1's aggregate comparisons. The GPU analysis also addresses the naive baseline's parallelization advantage. Its timings are explicitly estimated from PPO iteration costs, however, which limits the evidential strength of the stronger eightfold computational claim.
